title: Mental Health Causal Chains
text:
The Mental Health Causal Chains workspace is an internal CO-LUMINATE tool for capturing, reviewing, standardizing, and exporting youth-informed explanations of how lived social conditions shape mental health. It is designed to keep causal stories readable while also producing structured outputs that can be reviewed, refined, and carried into downstream analytical or reporting workflows. Within the builder, AI-improved wording is used specifically to harmonize bridge steps while leaving standardized mental health outcomes unchanged.

  
    Pathway library
    45
    Approved pathways already loaded into the internal workspace.
  
  
    Thematic domains
    9
    Domains spanning poverty, services, violence, spirituality, and related contexts.
  
  
    Wording views
    2
    Switch between AI-improved wording and original inventory wording.
  
  
    Export types
    3
    Workspace JSON, edge list CSV, and chain summary CSV for handoff and reuse.

section: Section A: Objective 2 - Depression Harmonization SAP
text:
Section A: Objective 2 - Depression Harmonization SAP

A1 Background and Rationale
This section defines the psychometric protocol for harmonizing depression measurement between the Shona Symptom Questionnaire and the Patient Health Questionnaire-9. The central challenge is not simple score conversion, but defensible alignment of instruments that differ in item format, recall period, and cultural grounding in a longitudinal multi-cohort setting.
The PHQ-9 is treated as the external benchmark for probable depression (Kroenke, Spitzer, and Williams 2001), while the SSQ contributes culturally grounded distress content that is relevant in Southern African settings (Patel et al. 1997; Haney et al. 2014; Chibanda et al. 2019). Objective 2 therefore treats harmonization as a staged psychometric program: item-set refinement, structural validation, invariance assessment, joint IRT calibration, and threshold comparison. In the finalized implementation, the theoretically derived SSQ-10 subset is retained as the main transportable SSQ configuration because it preserves the depressive core while avoiding non-specific distress items that weaken comparability with the PHQ benchmark (Putnick and Bornstein 2016; Woods 2009).


A3 Objectives and Estimands
Let \(Y_i^{PHQ} = \mathbb{1}\{PHQ9_i \ge 10\}\) denote the PHQ-referenced probable-depression indicator for participant \(i\).
The primary estimand is the harmonized binary endpoint
\[
Y_i^{H} = \mathbb{1}\{\hat{\theta}_i \ge \tau^\ast\},
\]
where \(\hat{\theta}_i\) is the calibrated latent depression score from joint PHQ-SSQ modeling and \(\tau^\ast\) is the selected latent threshold linked to the PHQ-9 reference scale.
Secondary estimands include prevalence alignment and threshold transportability:
\[
\Delta_p = \Pr(Y_i^{H}=1) - \Pr(Y_i^{PHQ}=1),
\]
where \(\Delta_p\) summarizes endpoint-prevalence drift under candidate thresholding strategies. Threshold comparison is not limited to a single rule. The anchored threshold linked to a PHQ-9 score of approximately 10 is compared with ROC-derived operating points and sensitivity- or specificity-targeted alternatives before a transport rule is selected.


A4 Study Design and Analytic Samples
The development sample comprises participants aged approximately 16-24 years with concurrent SSQ and PHQ observations available for joint calibration. The transport sample consists of SSQ-only records used to extend the harmonized scoring rule beyond the concurrent benchmark subset.
Eligibility is stage-specific:

structural-validity stages require complete item vectors for the candidate item set under evaluation;
IRT calibration requires valid item responses under the retained instrument configuration;
threshold comparison requires benchmark PHQ information;
endpoint assignment requires valid latent-score estimates from the final joint or fixed-parameter SSQ scoring workflow.



A5 Structural Modeling Strategy
Objective 2 evaluates three candidate SSQ configurations: SSQ-14, the theoretical SSQ-10 depressive subset, and the SSQ-8 comparison subset (Chibanda et al. 2019). Structural validity begins with Monte Carlo split-sample EFA using polychoric correlation structures and categorical-data retention criteria, followed by hold-out CFA using WLSMV estimation (Holgado–Tello et al. 2010; Wu and Estabrook 2016). Consensus item structures are identified across repeated split samples rather than from a single exploratory fit.
Let \(\mathbf{x}_i\) denote the ordinal or binary symptom vector and \(\theta_i\) the latent depression factor. The CFA measurement model is
\[
\mathbf{x}_i \sim f(\theta_i; \boldsymbol{\lambda}, \boldsymbol{\tau}),
\]
where \(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\) are factor-loading parameters and \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) are item-threshold parameters. Fit diagnostics are interpreted jointly rather than through single-cutoff rules, consistent with the revised psychometric workflow (Hu and Bentler 1999; MacCallum et al. 2002). Measurement invariance is then assessed across sex and age strata so that downstream thresholding does not rest on item structures that vary materially across key subgroups (Putnick and Bornstein 2016; Vandenberg and Lance 2000).


A6 IRT Harmonization and Threshold Derivation
Harmonization uses graded response models implemented in mirt (Samejima 1969; Chalmers 2012). For item \(j\) and category threshold \(k\),
\[
\Pr(X_{ij} \ge k \mid \theta_i) =
\operatorname{logit}^{-1}\left[a_j(\theta_i - b_{jk})\right].
\]
Separate instrument-level GRMs are used to confirm single-scale adequacy, after which a joint PHQ-SSQ calibration places both instruments on a common latent continuum. Latent trait scores are estimated using expected a posteriori scoring, and SSQ parameters from the joint model are exported as a fixed-parameter scoring engine so that SSQ-only records can be scored without refitting the full calibration model.
The primary applied threshold remains a clinically anchored \(\theta\) cutoff tied to the PHQ-9 test characteristic curve at approximately 10. However, the revised Objective 2 work compares this anchored rule with Youden-based ROC rules and constrained operating rules targeting high sensitivity or specificity before selecting the transportable endpoint definition for downstream Objectives 3-5.


A7 Performance Metrics and Uncertainty
Endpoint performance is summarized by:

sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, and accuracy;
AUC and Cohen’s \(\kappa\);
prevalence drift \(\Delta_p\);
subgroup consistency under alternate threshold strategies.

The workflow treats discrimination, calibration, and prevalence alignment as a joint decision problem rather than selecting thresholds on AUC or Youden performance alone. Uncertainty is summarized using resampling-based intervals and repeated-split diagnostics where appropriate (Efron and Tibshirani 1994).


A8 Planned Outputs and Reporting
Planned outputs are:

item-retention and structural-validity diagnostics for candidate SSQ configurations;
CFA, invariance, and DIF summaries for the retained SSQ-based depression structure;
joint IRT calibration outputs and threshold-mapping comparisons;
a fixed-parameter SSQ scoring engine for SSQ-only cohorts;
the final harmonized depression endpoint carried forward into downstream Objectives 3-5.

section: Section B: Objective 3 - Social Determinant Trajectories SAP
text:
Section B: Objective 3 - Social Determinant Trajectories SAP

B1 Background and Rationale
Objective 3 identifies developmental trajectories of childhood social determinants and evaluates how defensible those trajectories remain when longitudinal-information requirements are strengthened. This section therefore treats trajectory modeling as a scenario-comparison and reference-solution problem rather than as a search for a single intrinsically correct retained class solution (Muthén 2004; Nagin et al. 2016; Bauer and Curran 2003).
This framing follows the current harmonized trajectory workflow, which treats childhood social determinants as time-varying developmental processes and organizes them into early-childhood (0-5 years) and middle-late-childhood (6-12 years) windows (Hall and Posel 2019; Isabel Fortier et al. 2017; Simelane et al. 2025). The scientific aim is to preserve developmental timing while distinguishing robust trajectory structures from those that change materially when stronger repeated-measures requirements are imposed. Distal outcomes, including the harmonized depression endpoint and mediator variables, are used primarily for downstream class profiling after defensible reference solutions have been selected.


B3 Objectives and Estimands
The primary Objective 3 aim is to identify trajectory classes for key childhood social determinants across early childhood and middle-late childhood, and to compare retained class solutions across alternative longitudinal-information scenarios.
For model family \(a\), developmental window \(w\), and scenario \(s\), let \(C_{iaws}\) denote latent class membership with \(K_{aws}\) retained classes. The primary estimands include the retained class count \(K_{aws}\) and the class-proportion vector
\[
\boldsymbol{\pi}_{aws} = \left(\pi_{1aws}, \ldots, \pi_{K_{aws}aws}\right),
\qquad
\pi_{caws} = \Pr(C_{iaws}=c).
\]
Secondary classification estimands include entropy and the mean top posterior probability
\[
\text{Entropy}_{aws},
\]
\[
\overline{p}^{\,top}_{aws} =
\frac{1}{n_{aws}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{aws}} \max_c \hat{p}_{icaws},
\]
where \(\hat{p}_{icaws}\) is the posterior probability that participant \(i\) belongs to class \(c\) under model \((a,w,s)\).
Cross-scenario reallocation is summarized on the overlap sample
\[
\mathcal{O}_{awss'}=\left\{i: C_{iaws}\ \text{and}\ C_{iaws'}\ \text{are both observed}\right\},
\]
using the transition matrix
\[
T_{cc'}^{(awss')}=
\Pr\left(C_{iaws'}=c' \mid C_{iaws}=c,\ i \in \mathcal{O}_{awss'}\right).
\]
For distal profiling, the class-specific prevalence of binary distal variable \(D\) is
\[
\theta_{dcaws} = \Pr(D_i = 1 \mid C_{iaws}=c),
\]
estimated descriptively from assigned or weighted class summaries, and from BCH-ready branches where available. These estimands are defined because the Objective 3 workflow compares unrestricted, restricted, and stricter restricted branches rather than relying on a single fitted branch as the sole evidence source.


B4 Study Design, Analysis Populations, and Exposure Definitions
The study uses a longitudinally linked childhood-exposure file nested within the AHRI Health and Demographic Surveillance System context, with linked adolescent follow-up information available for distal profiling. The childhood-exposure file contains 5398 unique children overall, with 4318 entering the early-childhood analytic cohort and 5386 entering the middle-late-childhood analytic cohort.
Exposure histories are organized into two pre-specified developmental windows: 0-5 years and 6-12 years. All trajectory models are built on harmonized repeated childhood measures, with emphasis on preserving developmental ordering and avoiding post hoc redefinition of windows or determinant families.
The active Objective 3 model family set is:

ULWOM: univariate maternal co-residence trajectories;
ULWOF: univariate paternal co-residence trajectories;
UHSES: univariate household socioeconomic status trajectories;
JPA: joint parental residence pattern trajectories;
JMAES: joint maternal absence plus household socioeconomic status trajectories.

The active indicator set therefore includes maternal absence, paternal absence, and ordinal household socioeconomic status. A candidate overcrowding indicator was evaluated during harmonization but was not retained in the reported analyses because the available coding could not support a defensible cutoff and household-member irregularities risked undercounting children in some households. Its exclusion is treated as a conservative measurement decision rather than a weakness in the retained trajectory analyses.
Analytic eligibility is scenario-specific. Let \(\mathcal{T}_w\) denote the age set in window \(w\), and let \(R_{itm}\) indicate whether determinant \(m\) is observed for child \(i\) at age \(t\).
For univariate models, the within-window observed-occasion count is
\[
O_{iwm}^{(uni)}=\sum_{t \in \mathcal{T}_w} R_{itm},
\]
and the three univariate scenarios are:

Unrestricted: no additional minimum observed-occasion threshold beyond what contributes to the observed-data likelihood.
Restricted (\(\ge 2\) occasions): retain children with \(O_{iwm}^{(uni)} \ge 2\).
Restricted (\(\ge 3\) occasions): retain children with \(O_{iwm}^{(uni)} \ge 3\).

For joint models, a counted occasion requires all indicators entering the joint state to be observed at that age. If \(\mathcal{M}_j\) denotes the indicator set in joint model \(j\), the within-window complete-occasion count is
\[
O_{iwj}^{(joint)}=\sum_{t \in \mathcal{T}_w}\prod_{m \in \mathcal{M}_j} R_{itm},
\]
and the three joint scenarios are:

Unrestricted (\(\ge 1\) complete occasion): retain children with \(O_{iwj}^{(joint)} \ge 1\).
Restricted (\(\ge 2\) complete occasions): retain children with \(O_{iwj}^{(joint)} \ge 2\).
Stricter restricted (\(\ge 3\) complete occasions): retain children with \(O_{iwj}^{(joint)} \ge 3\).



B5 LCGA and Joint-Trajectory Strategy
Within each developmental window, the repeated ages are recoded to a local time score
\[
\tau_t = t - \min(\mathcal{T}_w).
\]
For each process \(m\) in class \(c\), the class-specific latent growth mean is
\[
\eta_{cm}(\tau_t)=I_{cm}+S_{cm}\tau_t+Q_{cm}\tau_t^2,
\]
where \(I_{cm}\), \(S_{cm}\), and \(Q_{cm}\) are class-specific intercept, linear slope, and quadratic slope means. The baseline LCGA specification fixes all within-class growth-factor variances and covariances to zero, including cross-process growth-factor covariances in joint models.
Maternal absence and paternal absence are modeled as categorical repeated indicators under a probit-threshold parameterization:
\[
\Pr(Y_{itm}=1 \mid C_i=c) = \Phi\left(\eta_{cm}(\tau_t)-\kappa_{tm}\right).
\]
Household socioeconomic status is modeled as an ordinal repeated indicator with levels low, middle, and high:
\[
\Pr(Y_{itm}^{SES} \le k \mid C_i=c)
=
\Phi\left(\kappa_{tmk}-\eta_{cm}(\tau_t)\right),
\qquad k=0,1.
\]
In joint models, a common latent class variable is shared across processes, but each process retains its own class-specific growth function. The JPA model combines maternal and paternal absence, whereas the JMAES model combines maternal absence and ordinal household socioeconomic status. Models are estimated in Mplus using TYPE = MIXTURE, ESTIMATOR = MLR, ALGORITHM = INTEGRATION, and INTEGRATION = MONTECARLO (Muthén 2004; Nagin et al. 2016).


B6 Class Enumeration and Model Selection
Class enumeration is conducted sequentially from \(K=1\) upward, with the current implementation permitting enumeration up to \(K=15\) unless the minimum class threshold is breached earlier. Class-enumeration decisions combine statistical and scientific criteria:

information criteria and neighboring class-count stability;
minimum useful class size and posterior separation;
substantive interpretability of class shapes;
consistency of retained solutions across analytic restrictions;
documentation against GRoLTS and SMART-LCA-aligned reporting standards (Nylund, Asparouhov, and Muthén 2007; Masyn 2013; Lissa, Garnier-Villarreal, and Anadria 2024).

The default minimum class threshold is \(5\%\) of the analytic sample for that model-window-scenario. When possible, the decision set includes the selected \(K\) and adjacent \(K+1\) solution for review, with lower adjacent solutions retained when \(K+1\) is unavailable, collapses, or fails admissibility criteria.
Because mixture solutions are sensitive to specification, local maxima, and sample restriction, retained solutions are also evaluated under structural sensitivity checks (Bauer and Curran 2003; Bauer 2007; Hipp and Bauer 2006; Watson et al. 2022). The current structural-sensitivity profiles are:

strict LCGA: all within-class growth-factor variances and covariances fixed to zero;
free intercept and slope variances within class;
free intercept and slope variances plus intercept-slope covariance within class.



B7 Cross-Scenario Comparison, Distal Profiling, and Missing Data
Cross-scenario comparison is treated as a core part of the Objective 3 inference rather than as a post hoc sensitivity appendix. For each model family and developmental window, the SAP compares:

analytic sample size;
retained class count;
entropy;
mean top posterior probability;
posterior range across classes;
minimum class proportion.

Class reallocation is summarized using overlap-sample transition matrices, same-label retention proportions, and alluvial diagrams built on the overlap sample. Because overlap-based alluvia quantify reallocation only among participants represented in all compared scenarios, total scenario-specific attrition is reported separately in summary tables and text rather than inferred from the alluvia alone.
Each model family and developmental window will have one defensible reference solution selected for downstream profiling. Under the current design, the default candidate reference branches are:

univariate: restricted (\(\ge 3\) occasions);
joint: stricter restricted (\(\ge 3\) complete occasions).

The distal-outcome layer is descriptive by default. Planned class profiles include probable depression, mediator variables, and contextual descriptive variables where relevant. Where model outputs support BCH weighting, BCH-based distal summaries may be reported as secondary analyses for branch-ready reference solutions.
Within each eligible scenario, repeated childhood outcomes are handled under the observed-data likelihood of the fitted mixture model. The restricted scenarios therefore change analytic eligibility rather than changing the missing-data model itself (Schafer and Graham 2002; Graham 2009; Parsons, McCormick, et al. 2024).


B8 Planned Outputs and Reporting
Planned outputs include:

retained-solution metric tables comparing sample size, class count, entropy, mean top posterior probability, and posterior range;
trajectory-profile figures, class-transition tables, and scenario-reallocation figures;
structural-sensitivity and reporting-checklist artifacts aligned with GRoLTS and SMART-LCA;
descriptive distal-prevalence summaries and BCH-based secondary distal outputs where available.

The main manuscript emphasizes analytic framework, scenario comparison, retained-solution defensibility, and key class-reallocation figures. The Supplementary Material carries the fuller class-enumeration ladders, expanded transition tables, extended trajectory panels, distal-prevalence tables, and audit artifacts. The results hub and trajectory comparison notebooks function as the full staging surface from which main-text and supplementary outputs are extracted.

text:
Section C: Objective 4 - Behavioral Mediators SAP

C1 Background and Rationale
Objective 4 identifies and prioritizes adolescent behavioral and proximal social pathway variables linking childhood social determinants to adolescent depressive symptoms. This section defines Objective 4 as a pathway-screening and mediator-prioritization analysis. It is designed to decide which pathway domains should be carried forward into later mediation-focused work, while keeping the current inferential target distinct from formal direct-effect or indirect-effect decomposition. This distinction matters in a harmonized multi-cohort platform where pathway variables, endpoint timing, and contextual exposure history all vary across source studies (Jörns-Presentati et al. 2021; Jakobsson et al. 2024; Rossouw et al. 2024).
Objective 4 treats the adolescent pathway block as a constrained but policy-relevant subset of a broader locally grounded pathway ecology. Candidate domains include material deprivation, violence, school-related adversity, social connectedness, and sexual-risk behavior, all positioned after childhood exposure windows and before the harmonized depressive-symptom endpoint (M. Mkhize, Westhuizen, and Sorsdahl 2024; Partap et al. 2023; Zimmerman et al. 2021).


C3 Objectives and Estimands
The Objective 4 study objective is to identify and prioritize adolescent behavioral and proximal social pathway variables linking childhood social determinants to adolescent depressive symptoms. The primary estimands are pathway-screening estimands derived from the joint pattern of upstream A-path support and downstream B-path evidence.
For pathway variable \(M_j\), the A-path model is
\[
\operatorname{logit}\left\{P(M_j = 1 \mid S_{0-5}, S_{6-12}, C)\right\}
=
\alpha_{0j} + \alpha_{1j}^{\top}S_{0-5} + \alpha_{2j}^{\top}S_{6-12} + \alpha_{3j}^{\top} C.
\]
For the depressive-symptom endpoint, the B-path model is
\[
\operatorname{logit}\left\{P(Y_i^H=1 \mid S_{0-5}, S_{6-12}, M_1,\ldots,M_7, C)\right\}
=
\beta_0 + \beta_1^{\top}S_{0-5} + \beta_2^{\top}S_{6-12} + \sum_{j=1}^{7}\theta_j M_j + \beta_3^{\top} C,
\]
where \(S_{0-5}\) and \(S_{6-12}\) denote childhood class-history representations, \(M_j\) denotes a candidate adolescent pathway domain, and \(C\) denotes the fixed covariate set. The primary B-path parameter for each pathway domain is \(\theta_j\), interpreted as the pathway-specific association with the harmonized depression endpoint after conditioning on class history and fixed covariates.
The principal study output is a prioritization judgement for each pathway domain based on upstream A-path support, downstream B-path support, robustness to fixed contextual adjustment, and coherence with the contextual pathway inventory.


C4 Mediator Definitions and Coding
The empirically testable adolescent pathway block comprises seven harmonized binary domains:

alcohol use;
ever having had sexual intercourse;
food insecurity;
lack of government grant receipt;
violence exposure;
low social support;
school disengagement.

These variables are treated as candidate pathway indicators rather than as already-identified formal mediators. They are harmonized from adolescent data collected after the childhood exposure windows and before the harmonized depression endpoint. Fixed covariate adjustment includes sex, adolescent age, rural residence, and calendar year of outcome measurement (Marlow et al. 2023; I. Fortier et al. 2017; Chilver et al. 2023; Mthiyane et al. 2025).


C5 Modeling Strategy
Objective 4 carries forward paired two-window class histories rather than using isolated class snapshots. The retained model families are:

ULWOM: univariate lived without mother;
UHSES: univariate household socioeconomic status;
JMAES: joint maternal absence and household socioeconomic status.

The strict restricted JMAES branch uses five early-childhood classes and seven middle-late-childhood classes. These families are interpreted as distinct but related representations of childhood social-determinant history. They are not pooled into a single exposure model; consistency across families contributes to pathway prioritization.
The class-history backbone is written as
\[
P(S_{0-5}, S_{6-12}, U^{(0-5)}, U^{(6-12)})
=
P(S_{0-5})
\times
P(S_{6-12})
\times
\prod_t P(U_t^{(0-5)} \mid S_{0-5})
\times
\prod_t P(U_t^{(6-12)} \mid S_{6-12}),
\]
with posterior class uncertainty carried into downstream screening rather than resolved through deterministic single-class assignment (Vermunt 2010; Asparouhov and Muthén 2014).
Within that class-history framework, three analytic layers are prespecified:

A-path screening of pathway-variable probabilities as functions of childhood class history and fixed covariates;
B-path models relating pathway domains to the harmonized depression endpoint after adjustment for childhood class history and fixed covariates;
jointly adjusted pathway models used to rank candidate pathway domains rather than to claim identified indirect effects.

All downstream regression stages use posterior-probability-weighted logistic models with participant-level cluster-robust standard errors.


C6 Mediator Prioritization and Phenotype Planning
Pathway prioritization is based on the joint pattern of:

A-path support across pre-specified primary and secondary hypothesis tiers;
B-path support across the three retained model families;
attenuation under nested fixed-covariate adjustment;
substantive plausibility in relation to the broader co-created pathway ecology.

Within that framework, food insecurity is the clearest candidate pathway, with violence exposure also prioritized and ever having had sexual intercourse retained as a supporting pathway domain. Alcohol use, lack of government grant receipt, low social support, and school disengagement remain part of the full evaluated pathway block and are reported transparently as lower-priority or weakly supported domains rather than removed from the screening record (Duby et al. 2022; S. Mkhize et al. 2022).


C7 Sensitivity and Robustness
Objective 4 places particular emphasis on nested fixed-covariate adjustment. Sensitivity analyses will assess whether attenuation of pathway-depression associations is driven primarily by age, calendar year, rural residence, or combinations of these factors. This reflects the design assumption that developmental timing and secular period are part of the data-generating structure rather than optional nuisance adjustments.
Additional robustness layers include:

pathway ranking by pre-specified primary and secondary A-path hypothesis tiers rather than nominal significance alone (Benjamini and Hochberg 1995);
complete-case main analyses with a separate 20-imputation maternal-baseline diagnostic branch retained as supporting specification work (White, Royston, and Wood 2011; Sterne et al. 2009);
interaction reviews for selected pathway combinations, especially violence exposure with school disengagement;
a contextual pathway inventory used to assess local relevance, partial measurement, and measurement gaps;
a working mediation-specification DAG used to summarize how the screening outputs inform later mediation-focused modelling;
reporting aligned to STROBE and AGReMA guidance (Elm et al. 2007; Moreno-Betancur et al. 2021).

The maternal-baseline imputation branch and working DAG do not replace the main screening estimands. They provide supporting evidence for later mediation specification by distinguishing stronger imputed maternal base candidates from auxiliary imputation variables and by separating baseline covariates, fixed contextual covariates, screened pathway domains, and broader conceptual downstream structural nodes.


C8 Planned Outputs and Reporting
Planned outputs include:

A-path hierarchy tables by hypothesis tier and model family;
B-path association tables for the seven pathway domains;
integrated pathway-evidence figures combining upstream and downstream support;
nested-adjustment attenuation reviews showing the effect of age, rural residence, and calendar year;
contextual summaries linking the measured pathway block to the broader co-created pathway inventory;
supplementary maternal-baseline diagnostic summaries and a working mediation-specification DAG;
a transparent shortlist of pathway domains prioritized for later mediation-focused analysis.

Section D: Objective 5 - Causal Mediation SAP

D1 Background and Rationale
Objective 5 carries forward the retained childhood exposure histories, the harmonized depressive-symptom endpoint, and the mediator shortlist from Objectives 2-4 into formal causal mediation analysis. The purpose is no longer pathway screening alone, but estimation of how much depressive-symptom burden is associated with selected childhood exposure histories overall, how much remains outside the selected adolescent pathways, and how much is carried through the retained mediator set (Pearl 2001; Imai, Keele, and Yamamoto 2010; Valeri and VanderWeele 2013; T. J. VanderWeele et al. 2016).
The finalized Objective 5 implementation is anchored on the strict joint-history branch requiring at least three observed childhood occasions per developmental window. The primary exposure is the joint maternal-absence plus household socioeconomic history because it preserves developmental ordering, represents co-occurring relational and material adversity, and yielded the richest defensible joint trajectory structure. Supportive univariate maternal-absence and household socioeconomic histories are analyzed within the same joint-history analytical sample.


D2 Objectives and Estimands
The primary Objective 5 objective is to estimate total effects, direct effects, mediator-specific indirect effects, and combined-set indirect effects linking childhood exposure histories to adolescent depressive symptoms.
Let \(H_i\) denote the childhood exposure history for participant \(i\), with \(h_0\) the reference history and \(h_1\) the comparator history; let \(Y_i\) denote the binary harmonized depressive-symptom endpoint; let \(M_{ij}\) denote mediator \(j\); and let \(\mathbf{M}_i=(FDSC_i, VLNC_i, ESXC_i)\) denote the joint three-mediator block.
The primary estimands are:
\[
\text{TE} = E\{Y_i(h_1, M(h_1)) - Y_i(h_0, M(h_0))\},
\]
\[
\text{NIE}_j = E\{Y_i(h_1, M_j(h_1)) - Y_i(h_1, M_j(h_0))\},
\]
\[
\text{Block NDE} = E\{Y_i(h_1, \mathbf{M}(h_0)) - Y_i(h_0, \mathbf{M}(h_0))\},
\]
and
\[
\text{Block NIE} = E\{Y_i(h_1, \mathbf{M}(h_1)) - Y_i(h_1, \mathbf{M}(h_0))\}.
\]
All reported effects are summarized on the risk-difference scale. The direct effect reported in the main manuscript corresponds to the combined-set block direct effect, because single-mediator direct effects vary by mediator model and are not directly comparable across separate single-mediator decompositions.


D3 Exposure, Outcome, Mediators, and Covariates
The retained Objective 5 exposure structures are:

primary joint maternal absence + household socioeconomic history: 5 early-childhood classes and 8 middle-late-childhood classes under the strict >=3 branch;
secondary univariate maternal-absence history: 4 early-childhood classes and 5 middle-late-childhood classes;
secondary univariate household socioeconomic history: 4 early-childhood classes and 7 middle-late-childhood classes.

The outcome is the harmonized binary depressive-symptom endpoint from Objective 2. The core mediator set carried into the main decomposition comprises:

food insecurity;
violence exposure; and
ever having had sexual intercourse.

The extension pathway record remains available for:

alcohol use;
lack of government grant receipt;
low social support; and
school disengagement.

Two adjustment sets are prespecified:

Base causal mediation estimand: sex, maternal age, and maternal education;
Context-adjusted mediation estimand: sex, maternal age, maternal education, adolescent age, rural residence, and calendar year.



D4 Analysis Population and Missing Data
The primary joint-history analytical sample consists of participants with:

an observed harmonized depressive-symptom endpoint;
contribution to the selected strict joint transition-history bundle; and
valid baseline information for the imputation and inferential stages.

The finalized Objective 5 implementation used an overlap sample of 1381 participants. Maternal baseline covariates were multiply imputed using 20 imputations with a maximum of 20 iterations and seed 20260414. Posterior-probability-weighted pseudo-records were then carried forward into the inferential models so that class uncertainty was retained rather than collapsed into deterministic class assignment.


D5 Estimation Strategy
Objective 5 uses transition-history g-computation on the probability scale. Total effects are estimated first for prespecified contrasts between selected childhood exposure histories. Mediator-specific decompositions then fit:
\[
\Pr(M_{ij}=1 \mid H_i, \mathbf{C}_i)
\]
through a logistic mediator model and
\[
\Pr(Y_i=1 \mid H_i, M_{ij}, \mathbf{C}_i)
\]
through a corresponding logistic outcome model. Standardized counterfactual means are combined to obtain total effects, direct effects, and mediator-specific indirect effects on the risk-difference scale.
For the combined three-mediator set, the joint mediator distribution is represented through sequential factorization rather than by summing separate indirect effects. This is necessary because mediator-specific indirect effects are not additive when mediators are correlated or represent overlapping components of the same adolescent pathway ecology (Tyler J. VanderWeele 2016).
The finalized pipeline used:

300 coefficient simulation draws for total-effect uncertainty propagation;
120 joint-block simulation draws for the combined three-mediator decomposition;
0 expanded-block simulation draws in the final retained pipeline.



D6 Prespecified Contrast Families
The primary total-effect contrasts compare adverse joint histories against lower-risk reference histories:

early childhood: Low Maternal Absence, Improving SES as the reference history;
middle-late childhood: Low Maternal Absence, Higher SES as the reference history.

The strongest prespecified contrast is the middle-late childhood comparison of High Maternal Absence, Low SES versus Low Maternal Absence, Higher SES. This is the focal contrast for main decomposition reporting because it showed the clearest adverse total-effect signal in the completed analyses.
Supportive univariate contrasts are prespecified around lower-risk and chronic-adversity anchors within the strict maternal-absence and household socioeconomic histories, and are interpreted as one-domain simplifications of the main childhood exposure story rather than replacements for the joint-history estimand.


D7 Robustness and Interpretation Rules
Objective 5 interpretation is intentionally conservative. Causal interpretation requires no unmeasured confounding of the exposure-outcome, exposure-mediator, and mediator-outcome relations after conditioning on the measured covariates (Imai, Keele, and Yamamoto 2010; Tyler J. VanderWeele 2016). Because these assumptions are demanding in observational data, the SAP applies the following rules:

positive total effects indicate higher depressive-symptom risk in the comparator history than in the reference history;
indirect effects are treated as pathway-consistent evidence when directionally coherent with the hypothesized mediator pathway;
indirect effects whose confidence intervals include 0 are interpreted as suggestive rather than conclusive;
context-adjusted estimates are stability checks on the base estimand rather than replacements for it;
secondary univariate analyses are supportive and do not displace the primary joint-history interpretation.

The finalized diagnostics showed stable model completion across imputations and adjustment sets, with total-effect and most mediator models using 1381 participants and 9347 pseudo-rows, dropping to 1365 participants and 9238 pseudo-rows when ever having had sexual intercourse entered the base joint mediator block.


D8 Planned Outputs and Reporting
Planned Objective 5 outputs include:

total-effect contrasts for the primary joint-history exposure and the supportive univariate exposure histories;
mediator-specific indirect-effect decompositions for food insecurity, violence exposure, and ever having had sexual intercourse;
combined-set direct and total indirect effects for the joint three-mediator block;
context-adjusted counterparts for the main total-effect and decomposition analyses;
model diagnostics and implementation manifests documenting imputation, simulation, and convergence.

Supplementary: Glossary of Symbols and Parameters
This glossary consolidates the core notation used in Sections A-D. Equation-specific parameter definitions remain embedded in the relevant sections.

Objective 2 Glossary

\(i\): participant index.
\(j\): item index.
\(k\): ordered-category threshold index for item \(j\).
\(Y_i^{PHQ}\): PHQ-referenced probable-depression indicator.
\(Y_i^H\): harmonized depression indicator.
\(\hat{\theta}_i\): participant-specific estimated latent depression score.
\(\tau^\ast\): selected latent threshold used to classify \(Y_i^H\).
\(\Delta_p\): prevalence drift between harmonized and PHQ-referenced endpoint prevalence.
\(\mathbf{x}_i\): vector of observed symptom item responses.
\(\boldsymbol{\lambda}\): factor-loading parameters.
\(\boldsymbol{\tau}\): CFA item-threshold parameters.
\(a_j\): GRM discrimination parameter for item \(j\).
\(b_{jk}\): GRM category-threshold parameter for item \(j\) at threshold \(k\).



Objective 3 Glossary

\(i\): participant index.
\(t\): developmental-time index within a childhood window.
\(c, h\): latent-class indices.
\(K\): total number of retained or candidate classes.
\(E_{it}\): observed exposure value for participant \(i\) at time \(t\).

\(\alpha_c\): multinomial logit intercept governing class-membership probability.

Objective 4 Glossary

\(S_{0-5}\): childhood trajectory representation for the 0-5 year window.
\(S_{6-12}\): childhood trajectory representation for the 6-12 year window.

Objective 5 Glossary

\(H_i\): childhood transition-history exposure for participant \(i\).

title: Objective 4: Behavioral Mediators
text:
The childhood social-determinant work in CO-LUMINATE identified distinct patterns of early and middle-childhood adversity. The next question was more practical: through which adolescent conditions do those childhood histories appear to connect most clearly to later depressive symptoms?
This objective therefore focused on pathway screening rather than on final causal decomposition. The aim was to identify which adolescent pathway domains were coherent enough, consistent enough, and well enough represented in the harmonized data to deserve priority in later mediation analyses.

title: Objective 4: Behavioral Mediators
text:
The childhood social-determinant work in CO-LUMINATE identified distinct patterns of early and middle-childhood adversity. The next question was more practical: through which adolescent conditions do those childhood histories appear to connect most clearly to later depressive symptoms?
This objective therefore focused on pathway screening rather than on final causal decomposition. The aim was to identify which adolescent pathway domains were coherent enough, consistent enough, and well enough represented in the harmonized data to deserve priority in later mediation analyses.

title: Objective 4: Behavioral Mediators
text:
What Was Screened
The current retained screening analysis used three childhood exposure-model families:

lived without mother
household socioeconomic status
joint maternal absence and socioeconomic status

Across those model families, the screening stage evaluated seven adolescent pathway domains:

food insecurity
violence exposure
sexual activity
alcohol use
lack of government grant receipt
low social support
school disengagement

These domains were screened in two ways:

upstream, by asking whether childhood social-determinant histories were associated with the pathway domain
downstream, by asking whether the pathway domain remained associated with adolescent depressive symptoms after adjustment for exposure history and fixed contextual covariates


This page is a public summary of the pathway-screening stage. The internal analytical report contains fuller technical detail, fixed-covariate sensitivity review, and the JMAES imputation specification checks.

title: Objective 4: Behavioral Mediators
text:
Screening Framework
The figure below shows the broad logic of the screening stage. Childhood social-determinant histories are treated as the upstream exposure block, the seven screened adolescent pathway domains sit in the middle, and harmonized adolescent depressive symptoms are the endpoint.

title: Objective 4: Behavioral Mediators
text:
What We Found
The strongest overall pathway signal came from food insecurity. It combined the clearest evidence that childhood adversity histories were linked to the pathway itself with the clearest evidence that the pathway was linked to adolescent depressive symptoms.
Violence exposure was the next strongest candidate. Its upstream patterning was narrower than food insecurity, but its downstream association with depressive symptoms remained strong enough to keep it central in the interpretation.
Sexual activity remained relevant as a supporting pathway. Its downstream association was visible, but its upstream support was more limited, so it was retained more cautiously than the two leading domains.
Alcohol use and lack of government grant receipt showed weaker or less stable support in the retained screening set. Low social support and school disengagement were also screened and reported, but neither showed enough upstream or downstream support to enter the core prioritised set.

  
  Figure. Pathway evidence summary across the strict restricted screening set. Panel A shows supported upstream contrasts out of the total prespecified contrasts for each screened pathway and exposure-model family. Panel B shows the share of model families with 95% confidence intervals excluding the null, with point size tracking the median adjusted odds ratio across families. Panel C shows the pathways taken forward for interpretation based on combined upstream patterning and downstream support, while the upper panels retain the lower-priority screened domains as part of the full screening record.

title: Objective 4: Behavioral Mediators
text:
Main Recommendation
The current recommendation is:

carry food insecurity forward as the clearest candidate pathway for formal mediation follow-up
retain violence exposure as the next strongest candidate pathway
keep sexual activity as a supporting pathway domain
treat alcohol use and lack of government grant receipt more cautiously or reserve them for extended analyses

Internal sensitivity checks on the strict JMAES branch did not materially change that ordering, so the pathway priorities shown here remain the preferred summary for broad review.

title: Objective 4: Behavioral Mediators
text:
What This Means For CO-LUMINATE
For the broader CO-LUMINATE program, this work does not claim that a single pathway explains the relationship between childhood adversity and adolescent depression. Instead, it identifies where the current harmonized data give the clearest and most credible signals.
Taken together, the current evidence points to food insecurity and violence exposure as the strongest practical targets for the next-stage mediation work, while also showing that some pathway indicators are better interpreted as partial markers of a wider social ecology rather than as complete standalone mechanisms.

Project Overview
CO-LUMINATE leverages the Africa Health Research Institute (AHRI) Health and Demographic Surveillance System (HDSS) to create a longitudinal linked dataset of 5,279 adolescents and young people. The dataset supports analysis of how social determinants of mental health, including socioeconomic status (SES) and caregiver co-residency, relate to depressive symptoms over time.
The project also uses a structured co-creation model with 11 Youth Co-Creators (YCC), who contribute meaningful thought leadership to refine, guide, and nuance the research process and interpretation.

title: Objective 2: Depression Harmonization
text:
CO-LUMINATE uses more than one mental-health instrument across studies and cohorts. The Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) is a conventional depression-focused reference measure, while the Shona Symptom Questionnaire captures a broader common mental distress space using culturally grounded binary items. Because those tools differ in content, response format, and construct emphasis, raw scores and raw cutoffs cannot be assumed to mean the same thing across instruments.
This psychometric work therefore asked a practical question: can we define a defensible depression-oriented endpoint that preserves the PHQ-9 benchmark while still allowing transport into cohorts where only SSQ items are available?

title: Objective 2: Depression Harmonization
text:
Data And Instruments
The harmonization-ready development sample comprised 843 adolescents and young adults with concurrent baseline SSQ and PHQ measurement. The work compared four instrument configurations:

the PHQ-9 as the depression-oriented reference benchmark
the original SSQ-14
a theory-refined SSQ-10 focused on depressive content
the shorter SSQ-08 subset

The central goal was not only to find a stable factor structure, but to identify which SSQ form best preserved a depression-focused latent trait suitable for later harmonization and downstream analysis.

title: Objective 2: Depression Harmonization
text:
What We Found
The main structural result was that the PHQ-9 remained a defensible depression-oriented reference, while the SSQ-10 emerged as the strongest retained local instrument for depression-focused harmonization. The full SSQ-14 carried broader common-distress content than was ideal for a transportable depression endpoint, and the SSQ-08 discarded too much of the more stable depressive core.

  

The retained SSQ-10 solution was analytically attractive because it preserved the strongest depressive content while avoiding the broader, more weakly targeted distress content that made the SSQ-14 harder to use as a depression endpoint. That made the SSQ-10 the most credible local instrument to carry into shared-scale harmonization.

title: Objective 2: Depression Harmonization
text:
Harmonization And Thresholding
The thresholding problem turned out to be as important as the retained instrument. Naive ROC-balanced SSQ cutoffs performed reasonably in discrimination terms, but they materially inflated the implied burden of depression relative to the PHQ-9 benchmark. In other words, a rule could look statistically appealing while still producing a public-health story that was too liberal to be credible for transport.
The more defensible solution came from Item Response Theory calibration. By placing PHQ-9 and SSQ-10 items on a shared latent scale, the analysis supported a clinically interpretable thresholding strategy tied back to the PHQ-9 reference. For cohorts where PHQ items are unavailable, the fixed-parameter SSQ-only scoring engine provided the most practical transport route.

  

The retained threshold strategy is therefore conservative by design. It favors a transportable SSQ-only engine that keeps estimated case burden close to the PHQ-9 benchmark rather than maximizing sensitivity at the cost of implausibly high prevalence.

title: Objective 2: Depression Harmonization
text:
Main Recommendation
The current recommendation is:

retain the SSQ-10 as the local depression-focused instrument
retain the joint PHQ-plus-SSQ IRT model as the harmonization reference standard
avoid naive raw-score thresholding as the main interpretation
carry forward the fixed-parameter SSQ-only scoring engine for cohorts without PHQ items

This combination provides the best balance between conceptual coherence, statistical defensibility, and practical transport into later developmental and causal analyses.

title: Objective 2: Depression Harmonization
text:
What This Means For CO-LUMINATE
For the broader CO-LUMINATE program, this work does not simply choose a questionnaire. It defines how depression should be represented when studies rely on different instruments. That matters for burden estimation, subgroup comparison, and any later work that treats depression as an outcome, a screening construct, or part of a harmonized longitudinal endpoint.
Taken together, these results indicate that the SSQ-10 can serve as the local bridge to a defensible depression-oriented endpoint, but only when interpreted through the harmonized thresholding strategy rather than through a raw SSQ cutoff carried over uncritically from another context.

title: Objective 1: Youth Co-Creation
text:
Abstract
This deliverable captures the youth co-creation workstream that informs hypothesis generation, lay DAG development, interpretation, and dissemination across the CO-LUMINATE study. In the private rebuild, the work is organized in two linked phases:

a pre-secondary analysis phase that develops a youth-informed pathway inventory and conceptual framing before formal modeling
a post-secondary analysis phase that uses youth interpretation to contextualize findings and strengthen stakeholder-facing communication

Together, these phases ensure that the technical analytical sequence remains locally grounded without turning the co-creation workstream into a separate modeled dataset.

Keywords

title: Objective 1: Youth Co-Creation
text:
Pre-Secondary Analysis
The pre-secondary analysis phase establishes the interpretive foundations for the later quantitative work. Following an inception workshop, Youth Advisory Group members contribute photo diaries, group-based narrative building, and a co-developed lay DAG describing how everyday social stressors may shape emotional distress among young people in the AHRI surveillance setting.
This phase contributes a contextual pathway inventory rather than a separate statistical dataset. The inventory identifies locally salient domains that help explain how structural disadvantage may become embodied as distress, including food strain, unsafe home and community environments, substance-related risk, school adversity, weak social connectedness, family separation, service-access barriers, and spiritual or cultural support.
That inventory then provides contextual grounding for the later behavioral mediator analysis. It helps justify why certain adolescent pathway variables were prioritized, clarifies what those measured variables do and do not capture, and keeps interpretation anchored in adolescents’ own accounts of how disadvantage becomes distress.

Full Pathway Inventory
The full contextual pathway inventory is shown below so the entire youth-informed pathway landscape is visible on this page rather than only a shortened subset.





Inventory domain
Inventory support
Contribution to later pathway screening
Current analytical capture




Food insecurity and material deprivation
Repeated pathways link poverty, crop loss, theft, mine closure, and household financial strain to food stress, worry, and poor mental health.
Provides strong local support for food insecurity as a proximal adolescent pathway domain and for interpreting it as one indicator of broader material deprivation.
Directly operationalized as food insecurity.


Violence exposure and unsafe environments
Inventory pathways repeatedly connect domestic violence, unsafe community spaces, taverns, crime, and substance-related insecurity to distress and poor mental health.
Provides strong local support for violence exposure as a pathway domain and for interpreting it as part of a wider insecurity ecology.
Directly operationalized as violence exposure.


Alcohol use and substance-related risk
Inventory pathways connect unsafe school and community environments, peer influence, financial strain, and substance use to emotional distress and poor mental health.
Provides direct contextual support for alcohol use as one observable component of broader substance-related and risk-exposure pathways.
Directly operationalized as alcohol use.


Sexual debut and broader adolescent risk ecology
Inventory pathways describe truancy, unsafe spaces, peer environments, and adolescent risk behaviours that may cluster around early sexual exposure and emotional strain.
Provides indirect contextual support for sexual debut while indicating that sexual debut captures only one slice of a wider adolescent risk ecology.
Partially operationalized as ever having had sexual intercourse.


Social protection and government grant conditions
Inventory pathways describe poverty, mine closure, reliance on grants, and the ambivalent social meaning of grant dependence, including stigma and eroded self-esteem.
Provides cautious support for social protection conditions as a pathway domain while indicating that grant-related experiences may be both protective and strained.
Partially operationalized as lack of government grant receipt.


School climate and educational pathway conditions
Inventory pathways highlight lack of school fencing, physical punishment, unsafe school environments, and early learning opportunities.
Shows that important school-related pathways are locally salient but only partly captured by the current pathway block.
Not directly harmonized in the present manuscript.


Family separation and migration-related stress
Inventory pathways connect migration for work and family separation to loneliness, insecurity, stress, and poor mental health.
Shows that migration-linked family separation is locally salient but outside the measured pathway block.
Not directly harmonized in the present manuscript.


Housing quality and water insecurity
Inventory pathways connect poor housing, water scarcity, hygiene constraints, bullying, and shame to emotional distress.
Shows that housing and water conditions form part of the broader pathway ecology but are not represented in the current analytic dataset.
Not directly harmonized in the present manuscript.


Social connectedness and community inclusion or exclusion
Inventory pathways describe community cohesion, exclusion from shared resources, low social connectedness, fear of stigma, and reduced help-seeking.
Shows that social-capital and exclusion pathways remain important contextual processes beyond the present measured variables.
Not directly harmonized in the present manuscript.


Service access, care barriers, and stigma
Inventory pathways describe long clinic queues, stigmatising treatment, transport barriers, and unmet care needs.
Shows that service-access and clinic-stigma pathways are locally salient but not tested in the present empirical model.
Not directly harmonized in the present manuscript.


Religion, spirituality, and cultural support or strain
Inventory pathways include church counselling, prayer, rituals, fear of witchcraft, and conflicting belief systems.
Shows that spiritual and cultural resources or stressors shape adolescent mental-health pathways but fall outside the current harmonized variables.
Not directly harmonized in the present manuscript.


Environmental degradation and climate stress
Inventory pathways link pollution, mine-related land damage, dumping, extreme weather, and erosion to fear, grief, and mental distress.
Shows that environmental and climate-linked pathways are important contextual mechanisms but remain unmeasured in the current analysis.
Not directly harmonized in the present manuscript.





In practical terms, the co-created pathway inventory strengthens the later pathway-screening work in two ways. First, it supports the selection of policy-relevant pathway domains that can be tested in the harmonized dataset. Second, it documents the broader pathway ecology that remains outside the measured variables, which is important for interpreting later findings with appropriate restraint.


Secondary Data Constraints
The inventory also makes an important secondary-data limitation visible. Even after careful harmonization, the measured adolescent pathway block captures only part of the broader pathway ecology described by young people. Several locally salient domains, including housing and water insecurity, migration-related family separation, service-access barriers, and spiritual or cultural support, are not directly measured in the current harmonized dataset.
This matters because the available indicators were assembled retrospectively across different source cohorts rather than designed as a single shared pathway instrument from the outset. As a result, a variable labelled as food insecurity, social support, school disengagement, or violence exposure may preserve the broad substantive domain while still differing in wording, response structure, timeframe, or local meaning across contributing studies.
The co-created pathway inventory therefore serves two purposes at once: it helps identify which measured pathway domains are locally grounded enough to carry forward into later analysis, and it clarifies where the secondary-data platform remains incomplete. This is why the measured pathway block should be understood as a constrained but policy-relevant subset of a wider adolescent pathway system, not as an exhaustive map of all relevant mechanisms.

title: Objective 1: Youth Co-Creation
text:
Post-Secondary Analysis
The post-secondary analysis phase begins after the main quantitative results are available. In this phase, Youth Advisory Group members engage with the emerging findings through structured interpretation and reflection workshops.
This workstream is intended to:

refine the explanatory narrative around the quantitative findings
identify where technical results align with, simplify, or miss lived pathway experience
support dissemination materials that are legible to community and stakeholder audiences
maintain context-sensitive framing when the study moves from analysis outputs to interpretation and communication

This post-secondary phase does not replace the statistical analyses. Instead, it strengthens the interpretive bridge between the technical results and the broader community-facing meaning of those results.

title: Project Proposal
text:
Scope

Population focus: adolescents and young adults aged 13-24 years.
Data structure: linked longitudinal cohort and HDSS records.
Core domains: socioeconomic status, food insecurity, caregiver co-residency, and related social stress exposures.
Outcome focus: symptoms of depression measured repeatedly over time.
Co-creation: youth partners contribute to interpretation and relevance framing.

title: Project Proposal
text:
Study Objectives (Full Statement)

Objective 1: Youth Co-Creation. Co-create a shared understanding of how social determinants shape young people’s mental health through a Youth Advisory Group, and integrate youth-led input into hypothesis generation, lay DAG development, interpretation, and dissemination framing.
Objective 2: Depression Harmonization. Describe prevalence of depression in the CO-LUMINATE dataset by harmonizing depression measures across cohorts (including SSQ and PHQ-9 sources) and deriving transportable depression outcomes for longitudinal analysis.
Objective 3: Social Determinant Trajectories. Characterize social determinant trajectories across childhood windows, including early childhood (0-5 years) and later childhood (6-12 years), and identify exposure-pattern pathways linked to adolescent depression outcomes.
Objective 4: Behavioral Mediators. Examine behavioral mediators, including migration, substance use, and sexual behaviour, as pathway mechanisms linking social determinants to depressive symptoms, and prioritize mediator structures for downstream causal modeling.
Objective 5: Causal Mediation. Estimate direct and mediated effects of key social determinants on depression among young people using longitudinal causal mediation methods and context-sensitive interpretation informed by the youth co-creation workstream.

Curated linked analysis datasets with supporting metadata and documentation.

title: IRT Scoring Workspace
text:
What The Workspace Returns


SSQ10_Total_Score, the observed raw sum of endorsed SSQ-10 items.
Theta_Harmonized, the continuous harmonised depression score from the packaged IRT engine.
Depression_Binary, the harmonised research-use classification based on the stored threshold logic.
PHQ_Expected_Sum and PHQ_Prob_GE10, which map the harmonised score back to PHQ-oriented summaries.
Engine and cutoff metadata that record which threshold scope, threshold approach, and applied target were used for the returned classification.
A downloadable scored CSV for batch runs, while keeping browser previews compact and easier to read.

title: IRT Scoring Workspace
text:
Benefits And Boundaries

  Benefits of the workspace
  
    
      Supports consistent harmonised scoring across single-record and cohort-level workflows.
      Exposes both continuous and binary outputs so the same workspace can support different reporting needs.
      Makes threshold behavior visible rather than hidden, including subgroup-aware fallback behavior where relevant.
      Helps researchers reuse existing SSQ-10 data without rerunning the full psychometric calibration pipeline.
    
  


  Important boundaries of use
  
    
      The workspace is designed for harmonised SSQ-10 research scoring and is not a standalone diagnostic tool.
      Current production-safe engines share the validated 1-factor SSQ-10 scorer, so engine changes typically affect thresholds more than the latent theta itself.
      Packaged performance summaries come from the reference packaging sample and may not generalise unchanged to every cohort, language, or treatment context.
      If subgroup fields are missing or do not match stored threshold levels, the applied threshold falls back to the overall engine threshold.
